cards.b: A mark with length and direction; can be thick or thin, continuous or broken, contour or gestural.
How light or dark something is; builds form, depth and mood.
Hue, value and saturation; used for mood, focus and symbolism.
Surface quality; actual (can be felt) or visual (implied).
A flat, enclosed area; geometric or organic.
Three-dimensional, or made to look so using tone and perspective.
Parallel lines used to build tone.
Layers of lines crossing at angles for darker tone.
Strong contrast of light and dark for drama, as in Caravaggio and Rembrandt.
A line that follows the edges of a form.
The space around and between objects; drawing it helps accuracy.
Rubbing pencil or crayon over a textured surface to record texture.
Place the focal point on a line of a 3×3 grid, not the centre.
A row of squares from white to black to check your range of tone.

short.q: Describe how to make a drawn sphere look three-dimensional.
short.model: Add a smooth gradation from light to dark, with a highlight, a darkest area on the side away from the light, and a cast shadow beneath.

short.q: Explain why a drawing using only mid-grey tones looks flat.
short.model: Without very light and very dark areas, there is no contrast to describe light and form, so objects lack depth and solidity.
points: no sense of form or depth

short.q: Give two ways of creating visual texture.
short.model: Use hatching for fur, stippling for stone, dry-brush marks for wood, or take rubbings and draw them.

short.q: How can line quality change the mood of a drawing?
short.model: Thick, dark and jagged lines feel aggressive or tense, while thin, light and curved lines feel delicate or calm.

short.q: Why is composition part of visual language?
short.model: Where you place elements, their scale and focal point guide the viewer's eye and communicate your intention.
